lessons.title: Retail Arbitrage: Finding Clearance and Discounts
lessons.body: Retail arbitrage means buying discounted items from physical stores and reselling them online for profit. In Africa, this works well with stores like Shoprite, Game, Pick n Pay, and even local pharmacies. Your goal is to find items priced 50-80% off that have steady online demand. Start by visiting stores early on weekdays when clearance racks are freshly stocked. Check endcaps, bottom shelves, and the back of aisles where staff hide stock for later. Use the free app 'Jumia' or 'Takealot' to scan barcodes and see current selling prices. For example, if a blender costs R200 on clearance and sells for R450 on Jumia after fees, that's a good flip. Always calculate fees: Jumia takes 10-15% commission, plus shipping. A simple rule: only buy if you can triple your money. Keep a notebook or use Google Sheets to track what you buy and sell. Build relationships with store managersâask when new clearance comes in. In Kenya, check Naivas and Carrefour; in Nigeria, Shoprite and Spar. Avoid perishables and heavy items. Focus on small electronics, toys, kitchenware, and branded clothing. Start with R500 or 5,000 naira and reinvest profits. Don't buy everythingâtest one item first. Retail arbitrage is the fastest way to learn sourcing because you see the product before buying.

lessons.title: Online Arbitrage: Sourcing from Websites
lessons.body: Online arbitrage is buying discounted products from websites and reselling them on marketplaces like Jumia, Konga, or Facebook Marketplace. You never leave your chair. Start with deal sites: Amazon's 'Today's Deals' (for international shipping to Africa), Alibaba for bulk, and local sites like Bidorbuy in South Africa, Jumia's flash sales, and Kilimall in Kenya. Use price comparison tools like PriceCheck or Google Shopping to spot gaps. For example, a phone case on AliExpress costs $1 (about 15 rand), but sells for R80 on Takealot. After shipping and fees, you profit R40. That's a 266% return. But watch out for import dutiesâin Nigeria, customs can add 20-35%. Always check 'delivery time' and 'return policy'. Use a virtual card like Payoneer or Wise to pay international sites. For local online arbitrage, monitor Gumtree and Facebook groups for mispriced items. A seller might list a used laptop for R2000 when it's worth R3500. Buy it, clean it, relist for R3200. Use a spreadsheet to track: product cost, shipping, platform fees, and your selling price. Aim for at least 30% profit margin after all costs. Start with items you can inspect locally to avoid scams. Never pay via EFT to strangers; use cash on delivery or escrow. Online arbitrage scales fast because you can source from anywhere, but you must master shipping and fees.

lessons.title: Wholesale and Liquidation Sources
lessons.body: Wholesale means buying in bulk from manufacturers or distributors at lower prices. Liquidation is buying unsold or returned stock from retailers, often at 70-90% off. In Africa, wholesale hubs include: Balogun Market in Lagos, Mai 47 in Johannesburg, and Gikomba in Nairobi. For liquidation, check websites like Liquidation.com (ships to Africa), or local auction houses. For example, a pallet of 100 mixed phone chargers might cost R1500. If you sell each for R50, you gross R5000. After fees, you profit about R2500. That's a 166% return. But you must inspect before buyingâmany liquidation pallets have broken items. Always ask for a manifest (list of contents) and condition. Start with small wholesale orders: 10-20 units. Negotiate hardâask for 10-20% discount if you pay cash. Build relationships with wholesalers; they give better prices to repeat buyers. In Kenya, check Industrial Area for electronics; in Nigeria, Alaba International for electronics. For liquidation, join Facebook groups like 'Liquidation Deals Africa' or 'Wholesale Suppliers SA'. Use a scale to weigh items if buying by kg. Always calculate landed cost: product + shipping + customs + your time. A good rule: your selling price should be at least 2.5x your total cost. Start with one category (e.g., phone accessories) and master it. Don't mix too many products early. Wholesale and liquidation can make you rich, but only if you buy smart.

lessons.title: Thrift Stores and Garage Sales Strategies
lessons.body: Thrift stores (called 'mitumba' in East Africa, 'okrika' in Nigeria, or 'second-hand' in South Africa) and garage sales are goldmines for cheap inventory. You can buy branded clothing, books, electronics, and home goods for 10-20% of retail. In Africa, mitumba markets like Gikomba (Kenya), Owino (Uganda), and Kantamanto (Ghana) sell bales of used clothes. A bale of 100 shirts might cost 5,000 KES (about $40). If you sell each shirt for 300 KES, you gross 30,000 KESâa 500% return. But you must sort: 20% are damaged, 30% are low-value, 50% are sellable. For garage sales, go early on Saturday mornings. Bring cash and a friend. Negotiate bundles: 'I'll give you 500 rand for all these books.' Use the 'OfferUp' or 'Facebook Marketplace' apps to check resale values. In South Africa, check Hospice shops and SPCA thrift stores. In Nigeria, check Yaba and Surulere. Always wash and repair items before reselling. Take clear photos with good lighting. List on Jumia, Takealot, or Facebook groups. For clothing, steam iron and hang on a hanger for photos. For electronics, test and clean. A key strategy: focus on one categoryâe.g., only kids' clothes or only vintage denim. That builds your reputation. Don't buy stained or broken items unless you can fix them. Start with R200 or 2,000 naira. Thrift sourcing teaches you to spot value fast.

lessons.title: Estate Sales and Auctions
lessons.body: Estate sales happen when someone dies or moves, and the family sells everything. Auctions are public sales where items go to the highest bidder. Both are common in South Africa, Namibia, and Zimbabwe, but less so in West Africaâthere, you'll find 'auction houses' for cars and electronics. In estate sales, you can buy furniture, art, tools, and collectibles for 10-30% of value. For example, a dining table worth R5000 might sell for R800. You clean it, take photos, and list on Facebook Marketplace for R3500. Profit: R2700. At auctions, set a maximum price before you go. Don't get emotional. Use the 'Bidorbuy' or 'Invaluable' apps to check past prices. In South Africa, check 'ClareMart Auction Group' and 'Aucor'. In Kenya, check 'Phillips International Auctioneers'. Always arrive 30 minutes early to inspect items. Look for hidden gems: old watches, cameras, vinyl records, and African art. Bring a torch and a magnet (to test metals). Pay with cash or bank transferânever a personal cheque. After buying, you must transport the item. For heavy furniture, rent a bakkie for R300. Calculate all costs: bid price + transport + cleaning + platform fees. Your resale price should be at least 3x total cost. Start with small items: jewellery, books, small electronics. Avoid large furniture until you have a vehicle. Estate sales and auctions are great for unique items that sell for high margins. But do your homeworkâsome items are worthless.

lessons.title: Evaluating Profit Margins and ROI
lessons.body: Profit margin is the percentage of profit you make on each sale. ROI (Return on Investment) is how much you earn compared to what you spent. Both are critical. Formula: Profit = Selling Price - (Product Cost + Shipping + Platform Fees + Packaging + Your Time). ROI = (Profit / Total Cost) x 100. Example: You buy a phone for R1000, spend R50 on shipping, R100 on Jumia fees, R20 on packaging. You sell for R1500. Profit = 1500 - (1000+50+100+20) = R330. ROI = (330/1170) x 100 = 28%. That's decent. But aim for 30-50% ROI. If ROI is below 20%, skip the deal. Use a free tool like 'Profit Calculator' on Jumia Seller or a simple Google Sheet. Track every expenseâeven airtime for calls. In Africa, hidden costs include: customs duties (up to 35% in Nigeria), VAT (15% in SA), and transport to the courier. Always add 10% buffer for surprises. For wholesale, calculate per-unit cost. If you buy 100 units for R2000, each costs R20. Sell for R50, profit R30 per unit, ROI 150%. That's excellent. But if only 70 units sell, your ROI drops. So test demand first. Use 'Google Trends' to check if a product is seasonal. Never guessâmeasure. Keep a spreadsheet with columns: Item, Cost, Fees, Selling Price, Profit, ROI. Review weekly. Reinvest profits into higher-ROI products. The goal is to double your money every 2-3 months.

quiz.q: What does retail arbitrage involve?
options: B) Buying discounted items from physical stores and reselling online
quiz.explanation: Retail arbitrage is buying from physical retail stores at a discount and reselling online.

quiz.q: Which app can help you check online selling prices while in a store?
quiz.explanation: Jumia is a major African e-commerce platform where you can scan barcodes and see current prices.

quiz.q: What is a good rule for retail arbitrage profit?
quiz.explanation: Aim to triple your money to cover fees and risk.

quiz.q: Which store is mentioned for clearance in Kenya?
quiz.explanation: Naivas is a major Kenyan supermarket chain with clearance sections.

quiz.q: What should you avoid buying in retail arbitrage?
quiz.explanation: Perishables spoil quickly and are hard to resell.

quiz.q: What is online arbitrage?
options: B) Buying from websites and reselling on marketplaces
quiz.explanation: Online arbitrage is sourcing products from websites and reselling them online.

quiz.q: Which tool helps compare prices online?
quiz.explanation: PriceCheck is a price comparison website in South Africa.

quiz.q: What hidden cost can add 20-35% in Nigeria?
quiz.explanation: Customs duties in Nigeria can be very high on imported goods.

quiz.q: What payment method is safer for local online arbitrage?
quiz.explanation: Cash on delivery avoids scams and ensures you get the item.

quiz.q: What is a good minimum profit margin for online arbitrage?
quiz.explanation: Aim for at least 30% profit margin after all costs.

quiz.q: What is wholesale?
options: A) Buying in bulk from manufacturers or distributors
B) Buying one item at a time
quiz.explanation: Wholesale means buying large quantities at lower prices.

quiz.q: Which market is a major wholesale hub in Lagos?
quiz.explanation: Balogun Market in Lagos is known for wholesale goods.

quiz.q: What is liquidation?
options: A) Buying new products from factories
B) Buying unsold or returned stock at deep discounts
quiz.explanation: Liquidation is buying excess or returned inventory at low prices.

quiz.q: What should you ask for before buying a liquidation pallet?
quiz.explanation: A manifest lists the contents and condition of the pallet.

quiz.q: What is a good rule for wholesale selling price?
quiz.explanation: Aim for at least 2.5 times your total cost to cover fees and profit.

quiz.q: What are thrift stores called in East Africa?
quiz.explanation: Mitumba is the Swahili term for second-hand clothing in East Africa.

quiz.q: What percentage of a bale of clothes is typically damaged?
quiz.explanation: About 20% of items in a bale are usually damaged or unsellable.

quiz.q: When is the best time to go to garage sales?
quiz.explanation: Garage sales are usually held on Saturday mornings and the best items go early.

quiz.q: What should you do before reselling thrift clothing?
quiz.explanation: Washing and repairing items increases their resale value.

quiz.q: What is a key strategy for thrift sourcing?
quiz.explanation: Focusing on one category helps you become an expert and build reputation.

quiz.q: What is an estate sale?
options: A) A sale of new goods
B) A sale of a person's belongings after death or move
quiz.explanation: Estate sales sell personal property, often after a death or relocation.

quiz.q: Where are estate sales common in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Estate sales are more common in South Africa than in West Africa.

quiz.q: What should you set before going to an auction?
quiz.explanation: Setting a maximum price prevents emotional overbidding.

quiz.q: What tool can help check past auction prices?
quiz.explanation: Invaluable is a database of auction results for price research.

quiz.q: What should you bring to an auction to test metals?
quiz.explanation: A magnet can help identify ferrous metals and test for gold or silver.

quiz.q: What is the formula for profit?
options: D) Selling Price x Total Cost
quiz.explanation: Profit is selling price minus all costs.

quiz.q: What is ROI?
quiz.explanation: ROI measures the profitability of an investment as a percentage.

quiz.q: If you buy for R1000, spend R170 on fees, and sell for R1500, what is your profit?
What ROI should you aim for?
quiz.explanation: Aim for 30-50% ROI to make the effort worthwhile.

quiz.q: What hidden cost should you add a 10% buffer for?
quiz.explanation: Always add a buffer for unexpected costs like customs or transport.
